subject: biology
title: Year 10 Biology practice test
summary: A 60-minute end-of-year practice test covering all of Year 10 Biology, with 6 short-answer questions and worked solutions plus 20 multiple-choice questions with explanations.
body:
This practice test covers the whole Year 10 Biology course in the style of an end-of-year exam. Working through it under test conditions will show you which topics you know well and which need another look before you begin VCE Biology.

## How to use this practice exam

- **Time limit:** 60 minutes in total. Spend about 20 minutes on the 20 multiple-choice questions and about 40 minutes on the short-answer section.
- **Conditions:** work alone, with no notes or textbook. A calculator is allowed.
- **Answering:** use correct biological terms, show working for any calculation, and give units. For "explain" questions, give a cause and its effect, linked with words such as "because" or "so".
- **Marking:** the short-answer section is worth 34 marks and the multiple-choice section 20 marks, a total of 54. Mark your work against the worked solutions, then revise the lesson for any topic where you lost marks.
- All data in this test are made-up teaching examples.

## Topics covered

| Topic | Where it is tested |
|---|---|
| DNA structure, genes, chromosomes and protein synthesis | Short answer 1; MC 1–4 |
| Mitosis and meiosis | MC 5 |
| Inheritance, Punnett squares and pedigrees | Short answer 2; MC 6–7 |
| Variation, natural selection, speciation and evidence for evolution | Short answer 3; MC 8–10 |
| Cells, microscopes and membranes | Short answer 4; MC 11–12 |
| Body systems and homeostasis | MC 13–14 |
| Food webs, energy flow, nutrient cycles and human impacts | Short answer 5; MC 15–16 |
| Pathogens, the immune system and vaccines | Short answer 6; MC 17–18 |
| Genetic engineering, PCR, gel electrophoresis and DNA profiling | Short answer 6; MC 19–20 |

## Short-answer questions

### Question 1 (5 marks)

One strand of a section of DNA has the base sequence:

`5′ – T A C G G A T T C – 3′`

a) Write the base sequence of the complementary DNA strand. (1 mark)

b) This section is 9 bases long. How many amino acids does it code for? Explain. (2 marks)

c) A mutation changes the fourth base from G to T. Explain how this could affect the protein and the organism. (2 marks)

### Question 2 (7 marks)

Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive condition. Use F for the normal allele and f for the cystic fibrosis allele.

Anna and Ben do not have cystic fibrosis, but their first child, Chloe, does.

a) State the genotypes of Anna, Ben and Chloe. Explain how you know. (2 marks)

b) Draw (or write out) a Punnett square for Anna and Ben, and state the probability that their next child will have cystic fibrosis. (2 marks)

c) What is the probability that their next child will be a carrier? (1 mark)

d) Their second child, David, does not have cystic fibrosis. What is the probability that David is a carrier? Explain. (2 marks)

### Question 3 (6 marks)

Before the arrival of a new predatory bird on an island, a population of lizards had both brown and green individuals. The island's ground is mostly brown rock. Twenty years after the predator arrived, 90% of the lizards were brown.

a) Explain, using the steps of natural selection, how the population changed. (4 marks)

b) Part of the population was carried to a distant island on floating vegetation. Explain how, over a very long time, this could lead to a new species. (2 marks)

### Question 4 (5 marks)

A student uses a microscope with a 10× eyepiece and a 10× objective. The field of view is 2.0 mm in diameter. She counts 8 onion cells lying end to end across the diameter.

a) Calculate the total magnification. (1 mark)

b) Estimate the length of one onion cell in micrometres (µm). (2 marks)

c) She switches to a 40× objective. Calculate the new diameter of the field of view. (1 mark)

d) Name one structure she would see in the onion cell that is not present in a human cheek cell. (1 mark)

### Question 5 (6 marks)

In a grassland, plants store 50,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ of energy. Grasshoppers store 4,500 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹, and the frogs that eat them store 360 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹.

a) Calculate the energy transfer efficiency from plants to grasshoppers. (1 mark)

b) Calculate the energy transfer efficiency from grasshoppers to frogs. (1 mark)

c) Give two reasons why most of the energy is not passed on to the next trophic level. (2 marks)

d) A pesticide sprayed on the grass is not broken down by organisms. Explain why its concentration would be highest in the top predator. (2 marks)

### Question 6 (5 marks)

a) Explain how a vaccine protects a person from a disease without them getting sick first. (2 marks)

b) A forensic scientist has only a tiny sample of DNA from a crime scene. Starting from 1 copy, how many copies of a DNA section would PCR produce after 12 cycles, assuming the amount doubles every cycle? (1 mark)

c) Explain why gel electrophoresis can separate DNA fragments of different sizes. (2 marks)

## Worked solutions

### Question 1

a) Pair each base: T–A, A–T, C–G, G–C. The complementary strand is:

`3′ – A T G C C T A A G – 5′` (1 mark)

b) Bases are read in groups of three (triplets or codons), and each triplet codes for one amino acid (1 mark). 9 ÷ 3 = **3 amino acids** (1 mark).

c) The change alters the second triplet (GGA becomes TGA), so a different amino acid may be coded for, or the triplet may now code for "stop" (1 mark). The protein may then fold into the wrong shape and not work, which can change the organism's phenotype, such as causing a genetic disorder (1 mark). (It is also possible that the protein is unchanged if the new triplet codes for the same amino acid.)

### Question 2

a) Chloe has the condition, which is recessive, so she is **ff** (1 mark). She received one f from each parent, but Anna and Ben are unaffected, so each must also have a dominant F: both are **Ff** (carriers) (1 mark).

b) Ff × Ff:

| | F | f |
|---|---|---|
| **F** | FF | Ff |
| **f** | Ff | ff |

(1 mark for the correct square.) Only ff is affected: **1 in 4 = 25%** (1 mark).

c) Carriers are Ff: 2 of the 4 boxes, so **1 in 2 = 50%**. (1 mark)

d) David is unaffected, so he cannot be ff. That leaves the three boxes FF, Ff and Ff (1 mark). Two of these three are carriers, so the probability is **2 in 3 (about 67%)** (1 mark). A common error is to answer 1 in 2, which ignores the fact that we already know David is unaffected.

### Question 3

a) Award 1 mark for each step, up to 4:
- **Variation:** the population already contained brown and green lizards, due to different alleles.
- **Selection pressure:** the predatory bird hunts by sight, and green lizards are easier to see against brown rock.
- **Differential survival and reproduction:** brown lizards were more likely to survive and reproduce.
- **Inheritance and change over generations:** brown lizards passed on the alleles for brown colour, so over many generations the frequency of these alleles increased until 90% of the population was brown.

Note: individual lizards did not change colour; the population changed over generations.

b) The two populations are now **geographically isolated**, so there is no gene flow between them (1 mark). Different mutations, different selection pressures on each island and genetic drift change each gene pool separately until the populations are so different they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring: they are **reproductively isolated**, and a new species has formed (1 mark).

### Question 4

a) Total magnification = 10 × 10 = **100×** (1 mark)

b) Convert: 2.0 mm × 1000 = 2000 µm (1 mark). Cell length = 2000 µm ÷ 8 = **250 µm** (1 mark).

c) Magnification increases from 100× to 400×, a factor of 4, so the field of view becomes 4 times smaller: 2.0 mm ÷ 4 = **0.50 mm** (or 500 µm). (1 mark)

d) Any one of: **cell wall** or **large central vacuole**. (1 mark) Note: onion bulb cells are not green, so they do not have chloroplasts; do not give chloroplasts as your answer.

### Question 5

a) Efficiency = (4,500 ÷ 50,000) × 100 = **9.0%** (1 mark)

b) Efficiency = (360 ÷ 4,500) × 100 = **8.0%** (1 mark)

c) Any two (1 mark each):
- Much of the energy is used in **cellular respiration** and lost as **heat**.
- Energy is used for movement and other life processes.
- Not all parts of the organism are eaten (e.g. roots, bones).
- Some material is not digested and is lost in faeces.

d) The pesticide is not broken down or excreted, so it builds up in each organism's body (bioaccumulation) (1 mark). Each predator eats many prey over its lifetime, so the pesticide becomes more concentrated at each trophic level and is highest in the top predator; this is **biomagnification** (1 mark).

### Question 6

a) A vaccine contains harmless antigens from the pathogen (for example, a killed or weakened pathogen, or part of it). The immune system responds by making antibodies and **memory cells** (1 mark). If the real pathogen later enters the body, the memory cells produce a faster and larger **secondary response**, destroying the pathogen before the person becomes ill (1 mark).

b) Copies = 2¹² = **4,096 copies** (1 mark). Check: 2¹⁰ = 1,024, and 1,024 × 2 × 2 = 4,096.

c) DNA is negatively charged, so when a current is applied it moves through the gel towards the positive electrode (1 mark). The gel acts like a sieve: smaller fragments move through the pores more easily and travel further than larger fragments in the same time, so fragments separate by size (1 mark).

questions.prompt: What are the three parts of a DNA nucleotide?

options.A: A phosphate, a ribose sugar and a base
options.B: An amino acid, a sugar and a base
options.C: A phosphate, a deoxyribose sugar and a base
options.D: A phosphate, a deoxyribose sugar and a protein

questions.explanation: Each DNA nucleotide has a phosphate, the sugar deoxyribose and one of four bases (A, T, G or C). A is tempting, but ribose is the sugar in RNA, not DNA. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, not DNA.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of bases is correct in DNA?

options.A: A with T, and G with C
options.B: A with G, and T with C
options.C: A with U, and G with C
options.D: A with C, and G with T

questions.explanation: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine. C is a common mix-up: uracil replaces thymine only in RNA.

questions.prompt: What is a gene?

options.B: A section of DNA that codes for a protein
options.C: One of the four bases in DNA
options.D: A different form of an allele

questions.explanation: A gene is a section of DNA at a particular locus that carries the code for a protein. A chromosome contains many genes. D reverses the idea: alleles are different forms of a gene.

questions.prompt: How many chromosomes are in a human egg cell?
questions.explanation: Gametes are haploid, with one chromosome from each of the 23 pairs: 23 chromosomes. A is the diploid number found in body cells. C is the number of autosomes in a gamete, forgetting the sex chromosome.

questions.prompt: A cell with 8 chromosomes divides by meiosis. How many chromosomes are in each cell produced?
questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number, so each of the four cells has 8 ÷ 2 = 4 chromosomes. C would be the result of mitosis. D is tempting because meiosis has two divisions, but the chromosome number is only halved once.

questions.prompt: A plant with purple flowers (dominant, P) is crossed with a white-flowered plant (pp). Half the offspring are purple and half are white. What is the genotype of the purple parent?
questions.explanation: This is a test cross. White offspring (pp) must have received a p from each parent, so the purple parent carries p: it is Pp, and Pp × pp gives a 1 : 1 ratio. If it were PP, all offspring would be purple, which is why A is wrong.

questions.prompt: Red–green colour blindness is X-linked recessive. A woman who is a carrier has children with a man with normal vision. What is the probability that a son of theirs will be colour blind?
questions.explanation: A son gets his Y from his father and one X from his mother. The carrier mother (XᴮXᵇ) passes Xᵇ half the time, so 50% of sons are colour blind. B (25%) is the chance for any child before you know its sex, which is the tempting answer.

questions.prompt: Which is the only source of new alleles in a population?
questions.explanation: Only mutation creates new alleles. Crossing over and independent assortment create new combinations of existing alleles, which is why A and B are tempting. Natural selection changes how common alleles are; it does not create them.

questions.prompt: Species X and Y differ by 3 amino acids in a protein. Species X and Z differ by 15. What does this suggest?

options.A: X and Y share a more recent common ancestor than X and Z.
options.B: X and Z are more closely related than X and Y.
options.D: The three species are not related at all.

questions.explanation: Differences build up over time after lineages separate, so fewer differences mean a more recent common ancestor. B reverses the logic. The data compare relatedness and cannot show that one living species evolved from another, so C is not supported.

questions.prompt: Which is the best evidence that two populations have become separate species?

options.C: When brought together, they cannot interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

questions.explanation: The species definition depends on reproductive isolation: no fertile offspring in nature. A is tempting, but individuals of one species can look very different (e.g. dog breeds). Living apart (B) is only the first step in speciation, not proof of it.

questions.prompt: Why are cells small?

options.A: Small cells have a smaller surface area to volume ratio, which keeps substances inside.
options.B: Small cells have a larger surface area to volume ratio, so substances can enter and leave quickly enough.
options.D: Small cells do not need a cell membrane.

questions.explanation: As a cell gets smaller, its surface area to volume ratio increases, so exchange across the membrane can keep up with the cell's needs. A has the direction of the ratio backwards: small cells have a larger SA:V.

questions.prompt: Root hair cells take in mineral ions from soil even when the concentration in the soil is lower than in the cell. Which process does this?
questions.explanation: Moving ions against their concentration gradient needs energy, which is active transport. Diffusion (A) only moves particles from high to low concentration, so it would carry ions out, not in. Osmosis is the movement of water, not ions.

questions.prompt: Where does most absorption of digested food into the blood take place?
questions.explanation: The small intestine is lined with villi, which give a huge surface area and a good blood supply for absorbing nutrients. The stomach is tempting because a lot of digestion happens there, but little absorption does. The large intestine mainly absorbs water.

questions.prompt: On a cold day, blood vessels near the skin narrow. What is this called, and why does it help?

options.A: Vasoconstriction; less blood flows near the surface, so less heat is lost.
options.B: Vasodilation; more blood flows near the surface, so more heat is kept.
options.C: Vasoconstriction; it makes the muscles shiver.
options.D: Vasodilation; less blood flows near the surface, so less heat is lost.

questions.explanation: Narrowing of skin blood vessels is vasoconstriction, which keeps warm blood away from the surface and reduces heat loss. Vasodilation (widening) happens when the body is too hot, to lose heat. Shivering is a separate response by the skeletal muscles.

questions.prompt: In a food web, foxes eat rabbits and rabbits eat grass. Foxes are removed by a disease. What is the most likely short-term effect?

options.A: Rabbit numbers fall and grass decreases.
options.B: Rabbit numbers rise and grass decreases.
options.C: Rabbit numbers rise and grass increases.
options.D: Nothing changes, because foxes are at the top of the food web.

questions.explanation: With fewer predators, more rabbits survive, so their numbers rise, and the larger rabbit population eats more grass. C is tempting if you think only one step ahead without following the effect down the chain.

questions.prompt: What is the role of nitrogen-fixing bacteria?

options.A: They convert nitrate back into nitrogen gas.
options.B: They decompose dead organisms to release carbon dioxide.
options.D: They convert nitrogen gas from the air into ammonium that plants can use.

questions.explanation: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria, some living in legume root nodules, turn N₂ into ammonium. A describes denitrifying bacteria. C describes nitrifying bacteria, which is the most common mix-up because the names sound similar.

questions.prompt: Which statement about viruses is correct?

options.A: Viruses are bacteria that are too small to see.
options.B: Viruses can be killed with antibiotics.
options.C: Viruses can only reproduce inside living host cells.
options.D: Viruses are single-celled organisms with a nucleus.

questions.explanation: Viruses are non-cellular and have to take over a host cell to make copies of themselves. B is a very common misconception: antibiotics act on bacterial structures, which viruses do not have.

questions.prompt: A person receives a vaccine and, months later, is exposed to the real pathogen. Compared with the first exposure to the vaccine antigen, the antibody response is:
questions.explanation: Memory cells formed after vaccination allow a secondary response that is faster and produces far more antibody, often stopping illness. A describes the primary response, which is what happens the first time the antigen is met.

questions.prompt: In producing human insulin by genetic engineering, what is the job of DNA ligase?

options.A: To join the insulin gene into the cut plasmid
options.B: To cut the plasmid at a specific sequence
options.C: To copy the DNA many times
options.D: To translate the gene into insulin

questions.explanation: DNA ligase acts like glue, joining the insulin gene into the plasmid. B describes restriction enzymes, the most common mix-up. Copying DNA many times (C) is done by PCR.

questions.prompt: In a paternity test, a child's DNA profile shows bands at 120, 180, 250 and 300 base pairs. The mother has bands at 120, 200, 250 and 330. Which man could be the father?
questions.explanation: The child's bands at 120 and 250 match the mother, so the father must supply the other two: 180 and 300. Only man B has both. C has 180 but not 300. A has exactly the mother's pattern and none of the child's unexplained bands.
